title: Inertia and Entropy
hook: Drift can look like character failure until the system is opened.
counterintuition: Blame sounds decisive. Instead, inspect the screen and handoff that keep old behavior alive before treating resistance as a character flaw.
tryThisNow: Choose one recurring failure and name the artifact that keeps it alive: a screen, schedule, rule, queue, or handoff. Mark one redesign move beside it.
keyTakeaway: Inertia is structural drag and entropy is coherence loss. Good strategy stops scolding symptoms and changes the design that keeps resistance or drift alive.

breakdown.fastRead:
Nina opens a policy admin screen and sees why the conversion memo has failed for six months. The call-center script asks agents to promise a faster quote, but the screen still forces four legacy fields before a policy can move. Drag is information when the old path keeps winning.

Inertia is not always stubbornness. It can be an inherited path that keeps the old routine easier than the new one. Entropy is the slow loss of coherence when no one keeps standards, handoffs, and priorities aligned. Strategy has to treat both as structural facts. Blame cannot rebuild the route that keeps winning.
breakdown.deepRead:
Antoine stands in front of a hospital incident board while patient comments and a handoff log sit on a metal cart. The room wants a new service-quality campaign. He points to the incidents that happen during the same shift change and deletes the campaign slide. The problem is not that nurses forgot to care. The handoff design loses information under pressure.

That is the move: translate blame into structure. Inertia shows up when the current path has weight. The old screen, old incentive, old route, old job boundary, or old budget rule keeps pulling people back. Entropy shows up when coherence decays: standards soften, exceptions multiply, and yesterday's workaround becomes today's normal.

Blame cannot redesign the path that keeps winning.

Petra sees the older version in a university department. The course catalog still requires a sequence built around professors who retired years ago. The room grid makes new sections nearly impossible, and retirement dates explain why no one owns the old rule. Petra places the catalog beside the room grid before anyone proposes another recruitment initiative. The inherited path is the constraint. Until the rule changes, energy will keep sliding into frustration.

A useful diagnosis does not excuse poor performance. It makes improvement possible. If people are careless, train or replace them. But if careful people keep producing the same failure, look for drag and drift. The system is teaching them what to repeat.
breakdown.fullRead:
You can see the weak spot before anyone names it. Janek walks past a scrap bin at a manufacturing plant and finds three versions of the same shift standard taped to different machines. The calibration sheet is signed, but the gauges are checked at different intervals on each shift. A supervisor says people need discipline. Janek asks which standard should win, then marks one calibration rule in red and removes the others.

The visible move matters because entropy rarely announces itself as collapse. It arrives as extra versions, informal exceptions, silent handoffs, and small losses of fit. Each workaround can look harmless by itself. Together they make the plant harder to steer. Entropy wins when no one owns coherence.

What would change if you stopped asking, "Why won't they do it?" and started asking, "What makes the old behavior easier?" A form may ask for obsolete information. A schedule may reward speed at the wrong moment. A queue may hide quality problems until they are expensive. A rule may have survived because removing it was never anyone's job. The point is not to be soft on performance. The point is to locate the real lever.

Leila learns that at a public broadcaster. For weeks, the digital workflow plan looks clean in slides. Then she opens the editing queue beside the broadcast schedule and platform dashboard. Broadcast deadlines still get first claim on editors, so digital clips wait until the audience moment has passed. Leila must decide whether to run another training session or change queue ownership. She changes the queue. One editor owns platform-first clips before the broadcast cut is final, and the dashboard becomes part of the morning handoff.

There is a limit to the structural lens. Some leaders use system language to avoid hard choices about skill, accountability, or priorities. That is only another kind of drift. Structural diagnosis should lead to a sharper action, not a foggier excuse. If the screen creates drag, change the screen. If the handoff loses information, redesign the handoff. If a standard has decayed, name one owner and one rule.

Matthew sees the same pattern in a food bank network. Pickup schedules, volunteer texts, and expiry labels have stopped matching each other. Before, each site solved the mismatch locally and spoiled food kept appearing on Friday afternoons. After Matthew places the pickup schedule in the open, he changes the sequence: expiry labels checked first, volunteer texts sent second, pickups confirmed third. The work feels less heroic and more coherent.

Good strategy treats resistance and drift as facts to be worked with. Inertia tells you where the inherited path has weight. Entropy tells you where coherence is leaking away. The strategic response is not louder urgency. It is diagnosis followed by redesign.

examples.title: Nina Opens the Old Screen

planSpec.audience: a reader facing legacy insurer facing policy-system drag
planSpec.stakes: whether the next decision produces coherent action or another respectable-looking activity pile
planSpec.requiredBeat: Nina moves one concrete constraint to the center of the table and crosses out every action that does not address it using policy admin screen so the lesson happens as a visible action.

examples.scenario: Nina, the conversion manager, puts the policy admin screen where the laptop was supposed to go at a legacy insurer's call-center pod in Hartford. has a call-center script and conversion memo beside it. Agents are measured on faster quotes, but the screen still demands four legacy fields. She has to decide whether to retrain agents or remove the old fields that keep dragging every quote backward. The agents are already logged into the old screen for the morning shift, so the drag has to be fixed where quotes actually begin.
examples.whatToDo: Put the screen at the center, cross out training that leaves the fields untouched, and redesign the quote path before blaming agents.
examples.whyItMatters: The screen carries inertia. Changing speeches will not overcome a path that still makes the old behavior easiest.

examples.scenario: "Show me which part this fixes," Antoine, the regional hospital quality director, says in the shift-change room, tapping the incident board. Patient comments cluster around the same handoff log gaps near the nurses' station. He must choose between a service campaign and a redesigned shift handoff, then deletes the campaign from the agenda.
examples.whatToDo: Fix the handoff log and shift routine where the incidents actually form.
examples.whyItMatters: Quality drift is not corrected by a message when the information handoff keeps decaying.

examples.scenario: Petra, the department director, hears a fluorescent tube buzz above the catalog cart in the university registrar's annex after another enrollment review. She lays the course catalog beside retirement dates and the room grid. The rule that blocks new courses was built around professors and rooms that no longer exist, and she must decide whether to recruit harder or change the inherited rule. The fall registration deadline is taped to the cart, making the inherited catalog rule more urgent than another recruitment idea.
examples.whatToDo: Name the inherited rule as the constraint and change the catalog sequence before launching another recruitment push.
examples.whyItMatters: Inertia often survives inside old rules that no one chose recently but everyone still obeys.

examples.whatToDo: Choose one calibration rule, remove the rival standards, and make one shift lead responsible for keeping the sheet current.
examples.whyItMatters: Entropy is the loss of coherence. A single owned standard does more than another discipline speech.

examples.scenario: It took Leila three weeks to stop trusting the neat workflow deck. The editing queue, broadcast schedule, and platform dashboard show digital clips waiting until the audience moment passes. She must decide whether to train producers again or change who owns the queue.  In the broadcast newsroom at 9:10 a.m., as the digital workflow director, she can see the queue still rewards the old broadcast path even when everyone says the platform has priority.
examples.whatToDo: Give platform-first clips a named owner before the broadcast cut is final and put the dashboard into the daily handoff.
examples.whyItMatters: The workflow resists change because the old queue still has priority. Ownership changes the structure.

examples.scenario: Matthew asks what changes when the pickup schedule is placed in the open at the food bank warehouse on Friday morning. As volunteer coordinator, he sees volunteer texts arriving after expiry labels are checked. After he reorders the work, labels are checked first, texts go second, and pickups are confirmed third. The cooler doors open for the noon pickup window, so Matthew needs the sequence to protect food before local improvisation takes over.
examples.whatToDo: Rebuild the schedule around the expiry constraint instead of asking each site to improvise harder.
examples.whyItMatters: Entropy shows up as mismatched local fixes. A shared sequence restores coherence.

questions.prompt: A legacy insurer keeps missing quote targets after a new script is introduced. The admin screen still requires four obsolete fields before a quote can move. What is the best diagnosis?
choices: The screen carries structural inertia that must be redesigned.
Agents probably lack enthusiasm for the new script.
The company should add another conversion memo.
questions.explanation: The obsolete fields make the old path heavy. Another memo or attitude story misses the structural drag inside the screen.

questions.prompt: A hospital sees patient complaints cluster around shift changes. Leaders want a service-quality campaign, but the handoff log loses key details. What should they do first?
choices: Launch the campaign so staff know quality matters.
Redesign the handoff log and shift routine where the drift appears.
Ask patients to submit shorter comments.
questions.explanation: The incident pattern points to a structural handoff failure. A campaign may sound serious, but it does not repair the place where information decays.

questions.prompt: A university department cannot add modern courses because the catalog sequence depends on professors who retired years ago. Which action best counters inertia?
choices: Rewrite the inherited catalog rule that keeps the obsolete sequence alive.
Advertise the department more aggressively to new students.
Ask retired professors to endorse the current sequence.
questions.explanation: The inherited rule is the drag. Advertising does not change the path students and faculty still have to follow.

questions.prompt: A plant has three versions of a shift standard near the same machine, and scrap is rising. Supervisors want a stricter discipline memo. What would address entropy?
choices: Post all three standards in larger type.
Tell each shift to choose whichever version fits its habits.
Remove rival standards and assign one owner for calibration.
questions.explanation: The issue is coherence loss. One owned calibration standard attacks the drift, while bigger signs or local choice multiply the confusion.

questions.prompt: A broadcaster says producers resist digital change. The editing queue still gives broadcast deadlines first claim on every editor, so online clips arrive late. What is the strongest move?
choices: Change queue ownership so platform-first clips get capacity before the broadcast cut is final.
Run a workshop explaining that digital audiences matter.
Publish a weekly leaderboard of producers who upload clips.
questions.explanation: The queue structure preserves the old priority. Training and leaderboards may add pressure, but they leave the source of inertia intact.

questions.prompt: A food bank network finds spoiled produce every Friday. Volunteer texts, pickup schedules, and expiry labels are out of sequence. Which response fits the strategic move?
choices: Ask volunteers to be more careful with all texts.
Check expiry labels first, then send texts, then confirm pickups.
Add more produce categories to the weekly report.
questions.explanation: The failure comes from a decayed sequence. Reordering the work restores coherence; more categories or vague care does not fix timing.

questions.prompt: A manager says, "People just hate change," after a software rollout fails. Logs show the old tool remains faster for common tasks. What should you challenge?
choices: Whether users were warned enough times.
Whether the old tool should be praised publicly.
Whether the workflow design makes the old behavior easier than the new one.
questions.explanation: The logs point to structural resistance, not a simple attitude problem. If the old route is faster, scolding users will not shift the path.

questions.prompt: A city agency has five pilot programs that started strong but now use different intake forms, metrics, and handoffs. Leaders want a sixth pilot. What is the better evaluation?
choices: A sixth pilot may restore excitement by adding novelty.
The agency should first repair coherence across forms, metrics, and handoffs.
Different forms prove each pilot is innovating.
questions.explanation: The pattern is entropy: coherence has leaked away across programs. A sixth pilot adds scope while the existing system is drifting.

questions.prompt: A sales team misses follow-ups because the CRM, calendar, and renewal spreadsheet disagree. The director wants a motivational contest. What should happen first?
choices: Find and redesign the artifact mismatch that creates missed follow-ups.
Run the contest so people show more urgency.
Let each seller choose the tracker they like best.
questions.explanation: The mismatch is a structural source of decay. A contest can raise effort briefly, but it does not make the system coherent.

reviewCards.front: A team keeps repeating a failure and leaders blame attitude. What should you inspect first?
reviewCards.back: Inspect the structure: screens, schedules, handoffs, incentives, and inherited rules that make the old behavior easier.

reviewCards.front: A process keeps drifting even after reminders. What structure should you inspect?
reviewCards.back: Inertia is drag from an inherited path. Entropy is coherence loss as standards, handoffs, or priorities decay over time.

reviewCards.front: A process has several local workarounds. What strategic risk do they signal?
reviewCards.back: They may signal entropy. Each workaround can look harmless, but together they make the system harder to steer.

reviewCards.front: When is a structural diagnosis not enough?
reviewCards.back: When it becomes an excuse. Diagnosis must lead to a sharper redesign, owner, standard, or tradeoff.

reviewCards.front: A new training program fails while the old tool remains easier. What is the retrieval move?
reviewCards.back: Change the path that creates inertia. Training will not beat a design that still rewards the old behavior.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice diagnosing resistance and drift as structural facts. Find the artifact, rule, path, or handoff that keeps the failure alive, then redesign it.

ifThenPlans.plan: If users return to an old tool, then compare the two paths for speed, friction, and required fields before blaming adoption.
If standards multiply, then remove rival versions and assign one owner for the living standard.
If complaints cluster at a handoff, then redesign the handoff before launching a morale campaign.
If a habit keeps failing, then look for the default path that makes the old behavior easier.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, choose one recurring failure and identify the screen, schedule, rule, or handoff that carries it. Make one small redesign to that artifact.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, review one process for coherence loss: duplicate standards, stale rules, local workarounds, or unclear ownership. Remove one source of drift.
